level1.text: A car drives round the bend of a motorway slip road at a steady speed of $20\,\text{m/s}$. The radius of the bend is $80\,\text{m}$. How large is the centripetal acceleration of the car?
A runner runs round a bend of a running track whose radius is $36.5\,\text{m}$. Her speed stays the same in the bend, $8.00\,\text{m/s}$. How large is the centripetal acceleration of the runner?

A stone of mass $0.50\,\text{kg}$ whirls on the end of a string along a horizontal circular path. The radius of the path is $1.2\,\text{m}$ and the tangential speed of the stone $4.0\,\text{m/s}$. How large is the net force on the stone?

A car drives in a roundabout whose radius is $25\,\text{m}$. An acceleration sensor shows that the centripetal acceleration of the car is $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. How large is the tangential speed of the car?

The radius of the drum of a washing machine is $0.25\,\text{m}$. During the spin cycle the tangential speed of a garment at the rim of the drum is $15\,\text{m/s}$. How large is the centripetal acceleration of the garment?

A car turns left at a steady speed, and a passenger sitting on the back seat is pressed against the right-hand door. It feels to the passenger as if something were pushing him outwards. What explains this correctly?
level1.answer: The passenger's body tends to keep going straight, and the door pushes him inwards into the bend.

choices.text: A centrifugal force pointing outwards acts on the passenger and presses him against the door.
choices.feedback: There is no centrifugal force: no object pulls or pushes the passenger outwards. The force from the door points inwards.

choices.text: The passenger's body tends to keep going straight, and the door pushes him inwards into the bend.
choices.feedback: Correct: the body would continue straight, so the door pushes the passenger inwards and forces him into the bend. This force from the door is felt as being pressed outwards.

choices.text: No sideways force acts on the passenger in the bend, because the speed of the car stays the same.
choices.feedback: The speed stays the same, but the direction of the velocity changes. A change of direction is acceleration, so a sideways force is needed.

choices.text: The friction of the seat pushes the passenger outwards, because friction opposes the motion of the passenger.
choices.feedback: Friction opposes sliding relative to the seat. The passenger would tend to slide outwards, so friction points inwards.

level1.text: A cyclist rides round a circular bend at a steady speed. In which direction does the acceleration of the cyclist point?
level1.answer: Towards the centre, because the direction of the velocity keeps turning inwards.

choices.text: In the direction of motion, because the cyclist keeps moving forward along the path.
choices.feedback: An acceleration in the direction of motion would change the speed. Here the speed stays the same, and only the direction of the velocity changes.

choices.text: Away from the centre of the path, because the cyclist feels being pushed outwards.
choices.feedback: The feeling of being pushed outwards arises because the body tends to keep going straight. The acceleration still does not point outwards.

choices.text: Towards the centre, because the direction of the velocity keeps turning inwards.
choices.feedback: Correct: the change of the velocity points to the inside of the bend, so the centripetal acceleration points towards the centre.

choices.text: There is no acceleration, because the speed of the cyclist stays the same throughout the bend.
choices.feedback: Acceleration tells how the velocity changes, and velocity is a vector. When the direction changes, the velocity changes, even if the speed stays the same.

level1.text: A motorcycle goes round a circular bend at a steady speed, and its centripetal acceleration is $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. The rider goes round the same bend again at three times the speed. How large is the centripetal acceleration then?

level2.text: A cyclist rides through the bottom of a dip in an underpass at a steady speed of $8.0\,\text{m/s}$. The combined mass of the cyclist and the bicycle is $80\,\text{kg}$, and at the bottom of the dip the radius of the arc of the road is $16\,\text{m}$. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected. How large is the support force of the road on the bicycle at the bottom of the dip? Give the answer in kilonewtons.

A playground roundabout turns steadily so that one revolution lasts $5.0\,\text{s}$. A child sits at the edge of the roundabout, $3.0\,\text{m}$ from the centre. How large is the centripetal acceleration of the child?

A car of mass $1200\,\text{kg}$ drives over a hill at a steady speed of $12\,\text{m/s}$. At the top of the hill the radius of the arc of the road is $30\,\text{m}$. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected. How large is the support force of the road on the car at the top? Give the answer in kilonewtons.

A hammer thrower whirls a hammer of mass $7.26\,\text{kg}$ before the throw. Assume that the hammer goes round a horizontal circle of radius $1.8\,\text{m}$ and one revolution lasts $0.50\,\text{s}$. How large is the net force on the hammer? Give the answer in kilonewtons.

Students study how the tension of a string depends on the speed of circular motion. A small rubber stopper moves in a circle at the end of a string on a smooth horizontal table, and the radius of the circle is kept constant, $0.80\,\text{m}$. The force $F$ of the string is measured with a force meter, and the tangential speed $v$ is calculated from the time of one revolution. The data are sample data.

Draw the $(v^2, F)$ graph and fit a straight line through the origin to it. Read the slope from the line and use it to calculate the mass of the stopper. The tabletop is smooth and the string is horizontal, so the tension is the only horizontal force.

The answer box takes the mass of the stopper in grams.

On a wet test track a driver drives a car round a circle and increases the speed until the car starts to slide. In different trials the radius $r$ of the circle varies, and the greatest tangential speed $v$ reached without sliding is measured. The data are sample data.

The track is horizontal, and air resistance is neglected. For each row, calculate the coefficient of static friction $\mu_0$ with which the car only just stays on the track, and determine their mean.

The answer box takes the mean of the friction coefficient.

A student solved the problem: “A car of mass $850\,\text{kg}$ goes through a horizontal bend at a steady speed of $18\,\text{m/s}$. The radius of the bend is $75\,\text{m}$. How large a friction force must the road exert on the car?”

The student's solution: “Friction towards the centre of the bend and a centrifugal force outwards act on the car. The centrifugal force is $m\tfrac{v^2}{r} = 3672\,\text{N}$. The net force must point towards the centre and be $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$, so the friction must be the net force plus the centrifugal force: $F_\mu = 3672\,\text{N} + 3672\,\text{N} = 7344\,\text{N}$.”

a) Explain what the error in the student's solution is.

b) Calculate the correct friction force.

The answer box takes the result of part b) in kilonewtons.

A roller coaster car goes through the topmost point of a vertical, circular loop. The car is then upside down below the track, and the track presses the car. At the topmost point the normal acceleration of the car is $a_\text{n} = 1.5\,g$, where $g$ is the acceleration of free fall. Air resistance and friction are neglected.

In the diagrams $\overline{G}$ is the weight of the car and $\overline{N}$ the support force of the track. The arrow $\overline{F}_\text{kp}$ is a force named the centrifugal force, and $\overline{v}$ is the velocity of the car. All the diagrams are drawn to the same scale.

Which free-body diagram shows correctly the forces acting on the car at the topmost point of the loop?

choices.feedback: Here the support force has been drawn upwards like the support force of a floor. The track is above the car, so it pushes the car downwards. An upward $\overline{N}$ would give a net force of only $0.5\,G$, although the acceleration requires $1.5\,G$.

There is no centrifugal force: no object pulls the car upwards, away from the centre of the loop. In this diagram the forces cancel each other, although the car accelerates towards the centre, so the net force cannot be zero.
Correct: only the Earth and the track act on the car, and both forces point down towards the centre of the loop. The net force is $G + N = 1.5\,mg$, so the support force is $N = 0.5\,G$.

Velocity is not a force, so its arrow $\overline{v}$ does not belong in a free-body diagram. The motion does not need a force pushing forward: the car keeps its speed, and the forces only turn the direction of the velocity towards the centre.

level3.text: An icy road bends horizontally, and the radius of the bend is $60\,\text{m}$. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the ice is $0.10$. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected. What is the greatest speed at which a car can go through the bend without sliding? Give the answer in $\text{km/h}$.

A puck of mass $0.40\,\text{kg}$ is tied with a string to a peg fixed to a table, and it slides on the smooth table along a horizontal circle of radius $0.80\,\text{m}$. The string breaks if its tension exceeds $25\,\text{N}$. Friction is neglected. What is the greatest rotation frequency the puck can have?

A road designer dimensions a horizontal bend for a speed of $80\,\text{km/h}$. For safety, the friction of the road should not have to give the car a sideways force greater than $0.25$ times the weight of the car, so that the grip is enough also on a wet road. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected. How large must the radius of the bend be at least?

A roller-coaster car goes through a vertical circular loop. The speedometer of the car measured the tangential speed $v$ at the lowest and the highest point of the loop, and the centripetal acceleration $a_\text{n}$ was calculated from the speed and the shape of the track (table, sample data). The mass of the passenger is $60.0\,\text{kg}$. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected.

a) Calculate the radius of the loop from each row and their mean.

b) Draw the force diagram of the passenger at the lowest and the highest point. Calculate the support force of the car on the passenger at both points. How many times as large as the weight of the passenger is the support force at the bottom?

c) What is the smallest speed at the top at which the passenger still stays in contact with the car, when the radius is the mean from part a)? Is the speed in the table enough?

The answer box takes the support force at the top from part b).

The track of a motorway ramp bend is a horizontal circle of radius $130\,\text{m}$. The road is banked towards the inner edge of the bend at an angle of $8.0\,{}^\circ$ from the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the wet road is $0.40$. Air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected.

a) Draw the force diagram of the car and calculate the speed $v_0$ at which the car can go round the bend completely without friction. Give it in $\text{km/h}$.

b) Calculate the greatest speed at which the car can go round the bend without sliding when friction is taken into account. Compare it with the speed that the same coefficient of friction would allow in a horizontal bend of the same radius.

c) Justify in your own words why a banked bend helps.

The answer box takes the greatest speed from part b) in $\text{km/h}$.
